title: Campaign Ad

jokes.text: Bobby Newport mispronouncing 'campaign' as 'cam-pain' vs 'cam-pleasure'
jokes.setup: Bobby is introduced as the heir to a candy fortune who just entered the race and is immediately 70 points ahead
jokes.punchline: His first substantive line is a childish wordplay joke — 'cam-pain' vs 'cam-pleasure' — delivered with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: The pun itself is weak, but that's the joke — Bobby thinks this is clever. Perfectly establishes his dim, entitled, cheerful character in one line. High character integration: only Bobby would think this is a great opener. The wordplay is intentionally bad, which is the craft.

dialogue.speaker: Bobby Newport
dialogue.line: My campaign is going great. I'm having the time of my life. You could say I'm really enjoying the campaign... pleasure.

jokes.text: Bobby inviting people to line up for autographs and 'free Bobby bars' at a campaign event where nobody asked
jokes.setup: Bobby is supposedly running a serious political campaign
jokes.punchline: He treats it like a celebrity signing event and distributes his family's candy as if that's normal campaigning
jokes.explanation: Establishes the running gag of Bobby bars and his complete misunderstanding of what a campaign is. Character-specific and effective world-building comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Bobby's got the looks, the charm, the charisma. But you know what I've got? A comprehensive understanding of municipal code, a working knowledge of the Parks Department budget, and I've read every single binder in the planning office. And that, my friends, is sexy.

jokes.text: Bobby Newport offering free Bobby bars, repeating 'My dad made 'em'
jokes.setup: Bobby is a candidate for city council, ostensibly a serious political position
jokes.punchline: He promotes free candy bars and keeps crediting his dad as if that's a personal achievement
jokes.explanation: 'My dad made 'em' becomes a running gag that encapsulates Bobby's entire character — everything he has comes from his father and he's blissfully unaware this is embarrassing. The repetition amplifies the joke each time.

dialogue.speaker: Bobby Newport
dialogue.line: Of course, I'd be happy to sign something for you, uh... Leslee? Is it Leslee?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: It's Leslie.

dialogue.speaker: Bobby Newport
dialogue.line: Right, right, Leslie. L-E-S-L-I-E-E.

jokes.text: Leslie's talking head: 'I am a lifelong government bureaucrat who's well-versed in the issues. And those are the kind of sexy qualifications that win elections.'
jokes.setup: Leslie describes her opponent Bobby Newport — attractive, charming, family employs half the town, already 70 points up
jokes.punchline: She pivots to her own qualifications with completely unearned confidence, calling 'government bureaucrat' a 'sexy qualification'
jokes.explanation: This is excellent character comedy. The word 'sexy' attached to 'government bureaucrat' is a perfect Leslie Knope construction — she genuinely believes this is compelling. The structure is tight: build the bad news, pivot to self-delusion. High quotability. The joke only works with Leslie's specific brand of earnest obliviousness.

dialogue.speaker: Bobby Newport
dialogue.line: Wait, Leslie Knope is running for city council? Against me?

dialogue.speaker: Bobby Newport
dialogue.line: I didn't know that.

jokes.text: Bobby mispronouncing 'Knope' as 'Lope' and 'Nesney' even after being corrected, then asking if she wants it signed to 'miss lope or just Nesney'
jokes.setup: Leslie introduces herself formally to her political opponent
jokes.punchline: Bobby immediately mangles her name into 'miss lope' and 'Nesney' — two entirely different wrong attempts — then offers to sign something for her as if she's a fan
jokes.explanation: The escalation from one wrong name to a second completely different wrong name ('Nesney') is the comedic engine here. 'Nesney' is a beautifully absurd construction. Then the kicker: offering to sign it for her confirms he thinks she's a fan. Tight, well-structured, character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: April Ludgate
dialogue.line: Hey Ann, were you fired for sleeping with doctors?

jokes.text: Bobby insisting 'I'm pretty sure I'm running unopposed' even after being told explicitly he's not
jokes.setup: Leslie's team explains she is running against him for city council
jokes.punchline: Bobby dismisses it entirely: 'I'm pretty sure I'm running unopposed, right?' — checking with his aide as if reality might confirm his preference
jokes.explanation: The 'right?' tag — asking his aide to confirm a factually wrong belief — is a great character beat. Bobby doesn't process information that contradicts his worldview. Efficient, character-specific, and sets up the 'you've very opposed by me' line.

dialogue.speaker: Andy Dwyer
dialogue.line: My stomach hurts, my head hurts, my heart hurts. I think I'm dying, Ann. I'm pretty sure this is what dying feels like.

dialogue.speaker: Ann Perkins
dialogue.line: Andy, you're not dying.

dialogue.speaker: Andy Dwyer
dialogue.line: How do you know? You're not a doctor. Oh wait, you are a nurse. But that's basically the same thing, right? My left eye won't stop twitching. I think I have a brain tumor. Also, I'm pretty sure I saw a ghost this morning.

dialogue.speaker: Ann Perkins
dialogue.line: You saw a ghost?

dialogue.speaker: Andy Dwyer
dialogue.line: It was wearing a white sheet. Turned out to be a bed sheet. From my bed. I couldn't find it this morning and got really upset. Also, I haven't eaten since yesterday.

jokes.text: Leslie's comeback: 'No, you're not running unopposed. You've very opposed by me.'
jokes.setup: Bobby insists he's running unopposed
jokes.punchline: Leslie's grammatically mangled but completely earnest correction: 'You've very opposed by me'
jokes.explanation: Leslie's mangled grammar in the heat of trying to sound authoritative is a nice character beat — she's so indignant she loses the sentence. Mild laugh, functional.

dialogue.speaker: Andy Dwyer
dialogue.line: I've been experiencing some troubling symptoms. Occasional headaches, fatigue, and sometimes my left arm feels tingly.

dialogue.speaker: Ann Perkins
dialogue.line: Andy, those are just normal human experiences. You're not dying.

dialogue.speaker: Andy Dwyer
dialogue.line: But what about the tingly arm?

dialogue.speaker: Ann Perkins
dialogue.line: You probably slept on it wrong.

jokes.text: Bobby, immediately after being told Leslie is his opponent, cheerfully asking 'What do you guys do?' and offering Bobby bars
jokes.setup: Leslie's team has just spent the scene explaining who they are and that they are running against him
jokes.punchline: Bobby has retained zero information and resets to campaign-event mode, offering candy
jokes.explanation: The callback to the Bobby bars combined with his complete memory wipe is a great escalation of his character. 'What do you guys do?' after a full scene of being told is the comedic peak of this interaction. Economy is excellent — one question does all the work.

dialogue.speaker: Andy Dwyer
dialogue.line: No, I didn't hit my head.

dialogue.speaker: Andy Dwyer
dialogue.line: I hit the wall in the head area with my head area.

jokes.text: Leslie's dry closing line to the scene: 'I think we scared him.'
jokes.setup: Bobby has cheerfully wandered off offering candy to strangers, completely unfazed by Leslie
jokes.punchline: Leslie interprets his clueless exit as a sign of intimidation
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the scene. Leslie's misreading of Bobby's obliviousness as intimidation is both character-specific and ironic. Economy is near-perfect: four words do a lot of heavy lifting.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I hit my head pretty hard on the swing set.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Yeah, you were out for like twenty seconds. It was awesome.

jokes.text: April's opening line to Ann: 'Hey, Ann, are you still a nurse or did they fire you because you slept with all the doctors?'
jokes.setup: April approaches Ann at the office, apparently to ask for medical help
jokes.punchline: She leads with a gratuitous insult disguised as a casual inquiry
jokes.explanation: Quintessential April Ludgate — a casual, unprompted mean-girl opener with no warmup. The structure of the either/or question ('still a nurse OR did they fire you because...') makes it land harder. Character integration is near-perfect; this is uniquely April. The immediate pivot when Ann calls her out ('You wanna try that again?') adds to the rhythm.

dialogue.speaker: Andy Dwyer
dialogue.line: Yeah, I got hit in the head pretty bad, but you know what? I've been trying to remember things better, and I actually remembered my PIN code on the first try today.

dialogue.speaker: Andy Dwyer
dialogue.line: So who's the winner now?

jokes.text: April's corrected version after Ann calls her out: 'Hey, Ann, are you still a nurse? Because Andy's not feeling well.'
jokes.setup: Ann demands April try again after the insulting question
jokes.punchline: April's 'corrected' version is still completely flat and robotic — she drops the charm entirely, just stating facts
jokes.explanation: The callback lands because April makes zero effort to be warmer — she just removes the insult and delivers the most mechanical possible version. It shows she genuinely doesn't understand social niceties, or doesn't care. Good escalation of the April/Ann dynamic.

dialogue.speaker: April Ludgate
dialogue.line: Wait, health insurance? I thought insurance was just for cars.

dialogue.speaker: April Ludgate
dialogue.line: I don't have that either.

jokes.text: Andy's list of symptoms: headache, seeing double, song stuck in head, teeth hurt, also hungry
jokes.setup: Ann asks what's wrong with Andy
jokes.punchline: His symptoms escalate from plausible (headache, double vision) to absurd (song stuck in head, teeth hurt) to just basic human experience (hungry)
jokes.explanation: The comedic engine is the escalation from real symptoms to non-symptoms to just being a person. 'Also I'm hungry' as the final item on the medical complaint list is perfectly Andy. Ann's response ('some of those things are symptoms and some of them are just being a person') is the ideal straight-man button.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: In my dream scenario, Mr. Belvedere is my campaign manager.

jokes.text: Ann's response: 'Okay, well, some of those things are symptoms and some of them are just being a person.'
jokes.setup: Andy lists headache, double vision, song in head, teeth hurt, hungry as his symptoms
jokes.punchline: Ann's clinical straight-man response acknowledges the absurdity without losing her composure
jokes.explanation: Near-perfect economy: the line does double duty as medical assessment and comedic punchline. 'Just being a person' is a quotable, calibrated response that earns a strong laugh. The straight-man delivery elevates the absurdity of the setup.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: I have not considered it. I volunteer at the Fire Department. I fight fires.

dialogue.speaker: Chris Traeger
dialogue.line: You do?

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: No. But if there's ever a fire, I will be there with a gun and some increasingly angry buckets of water.

jokes.text: Andy describing his head injury: 'I did smash my head area into the wall area'
jokes.setup: Andy denied hitting his head, then is asked again
jokes.punchline: He qualifies with 'technically' and uses the vague locators 'head area' and 'wall area' as if imprecision makes it less bad
jokes.explanation: The 'area' hedge is a classic Andy construction — vague language used to soften an obvious fact. 'Head area' and 'wall area' are funny because they're redundant qualifiers that say nothing. Well-integrated character voice.

dialogue.speaker: April Ludgate
dialogue.line: Are you a drug addict?

jokes.text: April's dry explanation: 'Yeah, he was hanging up his gold record.'
jokes.setup: Ann asks how Andy hit his head
jokes.punchline: April provides context that raises more questions than it answers — delivered with complete flatness
jokes.explanation: The humor comes from April's affectless delivery making the absurd (hanging a gold record, somehow managing to concuss yourself) sound mundane. Sets up the gold record callback.

dialogue.speaker: Andy Dwyer
dialogue.line: Well, I was doing this thing where I was like, 'protecting my brain helmet,' you know? And I put my hands up like this, and I guess I didn't realize how hard I was gonna hit myself. So I was just like, 'whoosh,' and then my brain helmet made contact with the wall, and that's when I knew it was bad because usually my brain helmet is pretty 'indestructible,' but apparently it's not as indestructible as I thought.

jokes.text: Andy's non-sequitur pivot: 'Point is, I have a gold record.'
jokes.setup: The scene has been about Andy's concerning head injury — Ann is trying to assess him medically
jokes.punchline: Andy pivots from medical crisis to humble-bragging about his gold record as if that's the salient point
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes. Andy's priority hierarchy — gold record > possible concussion — is a perfect character beat. 'Point is' frames it as a logical conclusion to a conversation that had nothing to do with this. Economy is excellent. Gets a big laugh and is highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Andy Barton
dialogue.line: I was reading this encyclopedia and I got so lost in it, I didn't even realize three hours had passed. It was incredible!

dialogue.speaker: April Ludgate
dialogue.line: You fell asleep on the couch.

jokes.text: Ann correcting April: 'Hey, smart ass, yes, you can. You have insurance.' / April's counter: 'Insurance is for if something bad happens to your car.'
jokes.setup: Ann tells them they have insurance for medical care; April calls her 'smart ass' back
jokes.punchline: April genuinely doesn't know what health insurance is — she thinks insurance only covers cars
jokes.explanation: The symmetrical 'smart ass' exchange is a nice structural touch. The genuine ignorance about insurance (it's for cars) is funny because it's plausibly how April and Andy would understand the world. Character-specific and grounded.

dialogue.speaker: Doctor
dialogue.line: Is there anything else bothering you?

dialogue.speaker: Andy Dwyer
dialogue.line: No.

dialogue.speaker: Doctor
dialogue.line: You sure?

dialogue.speaker: Andy Dwyer
dialogue.line: Well, actually, now that you mention it, my knee pit area has been really itchy, I've been having these weird dreams where I'm falling, and sometimes when I sneeze, a little bit of pee comes out.

jokes.text: Andy adding: 'P.S. I haven't had it in years.'
jokes.setup: Ann points out they have health insurance
jokes.punchline: Andy casually reveals he hasn't actually had car insurance in years — delivered as an afterthought postscript
jokes.explanation: The 'P.S.' framing is a nice Andy-specific construction — treating a spoken sentence like a written letter. The revelation that he doesn't have car insurance adds another layer to the April/Andy financial incompetence characterization.

dialogue.speaker: Andy Dwyer
dialogue.line: My doctor says I have the health of a sixty-year-old man. I'm thirty-four. He also says I sound like a rattlesnake when I breathe. I don't know what that means, but it doesn't sound good.

jokes.text: Ann: 'Oh, my God, we used to live together.' / Andy: 'Yeah, you still got it for me.'
jokes.setup: Ann is horrified to realize Andy has been without insurance while she was his girlfriend and housemate
jokes.punchline: Andy interprets her existential horror as lingering romantic affection
jokes.explanation: Andy's misreading of Ann's distress as romantic is pure character comedy. Simple but effective. The 'still got it for me' is a great non-sequitur that reveals his ego and his obtuseness simultaneously.

dialogue.speaker: Andy Dwyer
dialogue.line: So I ate a candy wrapper yesterday, and I've been tracking its progress through my digestive system. I'm pretty sure I felt it pass through my stomach around 2 PM.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry Gergich
dialogue.line: Andy, you're not supposed to eat the wrapper.

dialogue.speaker: Andy Dwyer
dialogue.line: Well, I know that now, Jerry. But the important thing is, I'm documenting the journey. By tomorrow, it'll be out of my system completely, and I'll have a full timeline to present to my doctor.

jokes.text: Bobby Newport's second campaign ad: 'My family owns nine square miles of land in this town. And isn't my family what this town's really about?'
jokes.setup: A polished campaign ad begins
jokes.punchline: Bobby's pitch is essentially 'my rich family owns everything, so vote for me' — delivered as if this is a compelling civic argument
jokes.explanation: The rhetorical move of 'isn't my family what this town's really about?' is a sharp satirical take on dynastic politics — the Newport family's entitlement packaged as civic virtue. Consistent character work.

dialogue.speaker: Andy Dwyer
dialogue.line: I've been swallowing gum for 25 years. The doctor said I'm gonna die, but I'm gonna die with the cleanest insides.

jokes.text: Leslie's talking head about Ben's strategy: 'the most amazing campaign strategy ever thought of in the entire history of western democracy. Go, Ben, here's your great idea. We're all ready for it. And start.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is introducing Ben's campaign strategy idea with enormous buildup
jokes.punchline: The over-the-top intro ('entire history of western democracy') followed by the comedically functional 'And start' undercuts itself by being so performatively enthusiastic
jokes.explanation: Leslie's hyperbolic enthusiasm is perfectly in-character. 'And start' as if she's stage-managing a performance is a small but funny beat. The gap between the setup ('history of western democracy') and the delivery context (a small-town council race) is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Andy Dwyer
dialogue.line: So I've got high cholesterol, type 2 diabetes, and a really bad back. Oh, and I broke my thumb. Can you just... fix all of it? Like, everything?

jokes.text: Leslie's self-aware talking head: 'I'm running for office. I'm surrounded by my friends. My campaign manager and I are in love. This is exactly how I dreamed it would be when I was a kid. Except I wasn't 70 points behind and my campaign manager was Mr. Belvedere.'
jokes.setup: Leslie describes her dream scenario, which sounds perfectly happy
jokes.punchline: Two sudden qualifiers: she's 70 points behind, and as a child she dreamed of Mr. Belvedere as her campaign manager
jokes.explanation: This is among the episode's best jokes. The structure is textbook: a warm, dreamy setup punctured first by the real problem (70 points behind), and then by the deeply specific, absurd detail that as a child she dreamed of Mr. Belvedere as her campaign manager. That specificity is what separates this from a generic 'childhood dreams vs. reality' joke. Only Leslie would have planned a political campaign at age ten with Mr. Belvedere. The two-part deflation is also well-paced.

dialogue.speaker: Bobby Newport
dialogue.line: I'm just a regular guy, you know? I shop at the same stores everyone else does.

dialogue.speaker: Bobby Newport
dialogue.line: In fact, my dog is a rescue dog. Well, he was rescued from the Queen of England's personal kennel, but still.

jokes.text: Ben's David vs. Goliath framing: 'We are David. Newport is Goliath. This is our slingshot.' [beat] 'Yes, we'll write an inspiring op-ed piece.' 'No, the Pawnee-Eagleton high school basketball game.'
jokes.setup: Ben builds to a dramatic reveal with a biblical metaphor
jokes.punchline: Someone immediately guesses 'inspiring op-ed piece' — the least exciting possible answer — before Ben reveals the actual plan (a local high school basketball game)
jokes.explanation: The misdirect works on two levels: the wrong guess deflates the drama, and then Ben's 'big idea' being a high school basketball game is its own modest punchline. Solid structure, moderate laughs.

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: Donna, I think you might have some issues going negative.

dialogue.speaker: Donna Meagle
dialogue.line: Ben, I don't have issues. I have a strategy. If you assume the worst, you're never disappointed. And occasionally, you get pleasantly surprised.

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: That's not healthy.

dialogue.speaker: Donna Meagle
dialogue.line: It's worked for me for 55 years.

jokes.text: Ron Swanson's 'Present' response to Chris saying his name
jokes.setup: Chris cheerfully calls out 'Ron Swanson. How are you?'
jokes.punchline: Ron responds 'Present' — as if taking attendance, giving the least socially engaged answer possible
jokes.explanation: One word. One perfect word. 'Present' is Ron Swanson in a single syllable — acknowledging existence with zero warmth, bureaucratic precision used to dodge human connection. Character integration is near-perfect: only Ron would respond this way. Economy score is 10. Highly quotable, a fan-favorite moment.

dialogue.speaker: Ann Perkins
dialogue.line: I can't believe how negative this campaign has gotten. It's awful. Leslie and I used to be friends, and now we're just... I don't know, it feels like we're enemies and... wait, is this a Crayola marker?

dialogue.speaker: Ann Perkins
dialogue.line: Oh my God, this smells amazing. What color is this? Burnt sienna? I love burnt sienna.

jokes.text: Ron suggesting cutting the entire fire department and claiming he's 'personally put out several local fires at no cost to the taxpayer'
jokes.setup: Ron has joined Chris's budget-cutting meeting with public works
jokes.punchline: Ron's first suggestion is eliminating an emergency service, justified by his personal firefighting record as a cost-saving measure
jokes.explanation: Ron's anti-government ideology taken to logical extremes is always funny. 'I personally put out fires' as a justification for abolishing the fire department is a perfect extension of his worldview. Highly character-specific, absurdist but grounded in Ron's consistent philosophy.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: I don't care about the river dam project. I don't care about rivers. I don't care about dams. And I certainly don't care about your concerns. Good day.

jokes.text: Ron to the public works director: 'Look to the left. The right. Whatever. Are you the kind of doctor who gets hooked on his own drugs? I bet you are.'
jokes.setup: Ron has joined a bureaucratic meeting about budget cuts
jokes.punchline: Ron non-sequiturs into accusing the public works director of being an addict, then casually adds 'I bet you are'
jokes.explanation: This is a weaker Ron moment. The 'doctor on his own drugs' line is a bit of a non-sequitur that doesn't quite land because it's untethered from anything. Mildly funny for the sheer randomness, but not as well-crafted as his best moments.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: I crushed your dreams. That's what I do. I crush dreams and build dams. And we're all out of dams.

jokes.text: Andy's secondary list of ailments: rash in 'knee pit area,' tongue that doesn't taste on one side, ankles making a 'weird rattlesnake sound,' fuzzy things far away
jokes.setup: Doctor says Andy's concussion is mild and asks if anything else is bothering him
jokes.punchline: Andy unleashes a cascade of absurd and long-neglected medical issues including 'knee pit area' and rattlesnake ankle sounds
jokes.explanation: 'Knee pit area' is inspired — it's technically correct (the popliteal fossa) but described with Andy's characteristic vague anatomical language. 'Rattlesnake sound' for ankle crepitus is also very funny and specific. The escalating list structure works well, building to absurdity. Each ailment is distinct enough to land independently.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: Here's my strategy: I bet on every horse. That way, no matter which one wins, I'm a winner.

jokes.text: Andy telling the specialist doctor: 'I was reading an encyclopedia, and I tripped or fell over and hit my head or brain helmet.'
jokes.setup: The doctor asks what happened
jokes.punchline: Andy's hedged account (tripped 'or fell over') plus 'brain helmet' as his term for skull
jokes.explanation: 'Brain helmet' is an inspired piece of Andy's vocabulary — it's not stupidity, it's Andy's poetic logic. The skull IS a helmet for the brain. The reading an encyclopedia detail also adds a layer (Andy trying to self-educate). Highly quotable, strong character voice.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Jerry, you're going to be on Ben's team.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry Gergich
dialogue.line: Oh, okay.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Yeah, I figure if anyone's going to be a big negative, it might as well be you.

jokes.text: April's correction of Andy's story: 'Yeah, he sneezed and smacked his head against the wall.' / Doctor: 'That sounds about right.'
jokes.setup: Andy gave an elaborate encyclopedia-tripping story
jokes.punchline: April deflates it in one sentence (he sneezed), and the doctor accepts this with zero surprise
jokes.explanation: The doctor's 'that sounds about right' is the real punchline — his complete lack of surprise at the story implies he's seen enough of Andy's type. Two-part structure with April as deflator and the doctor as validator works nicely.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Look, being positive is better than being negative. Obama was positive, and he became president. Ben is negative, and he's stuck in a mid-level government job.

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: I'm not negative, I'm realistic.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: That's what negative people say.

jokes.text: Andy's expanded list of complaints to the doctor: rash in 'knee pit area,' tongue doesn't taste on one side, ankles make 'rattlesnake sound,' things far away are fuzzy, ate a Twix with wrapper and never saw the wrapper 'come out,' swallowed every piece of gum for 25 years
jokes.setup: Doctor asks if anything else is bothering Andy
jokes.punchline: A cascade of increasingly absurd and unrelated medical and non-medical complaints, each one more impossible to respond to than the last
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's comedic peak for the Andy storyline. Each item in the list is distinct and builds in absurdity. 'Knee pit area' is a clever parallel to 'brain helmet.' The Twix wrapper concern and 25 years of swallowed gum escalate from worrying to existential to completely Andy. The structure (doctor asks, Andy delivers, doctor is overwhelmed) is textbook escalation comedy. The variety and specificity of the items is what pushes this above a simple list joke.

dialogue.speaker: Optometrist
dialogue.line: Can you read the next line?

dialogue.speaker: Andy Dwyer
dialogue.line: Yeah, it says... W, uh... that's a middle finger, right? And then an E, another middle finger, and then... is that a Q or a 9?

dialogue.speaker: Optometrist
dialogue.line: Those are all the letter M.

dialogue.speaker: Andy Dwyer
dialogue.line: Oh, wow. Your font is really aggressive.

jokes.text: Andy's final addition: 'I broke my thumb on the way over here. Just fix me.'
jokes.setup: Andy has listed a dozen problems; the doctor is overwhelmed
jokes.punchline: Andy has a brand new injury sustained during the trip to the doctor, then summarizes all of it with 'just fix me'
jokes.explanation: The thumb acquired en route is a perfect comic escalation — Andy is so physically chaotic he broke something on the way to address being broken. 'Just fix me' as the button is excellent economy: it's a plea, a joke, and a perfect character summary. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: April Ludgate
dialogue.line: If you get glasses, I'm divorcing you.

dialogue.speaker: Andy Dwyer
dialogue.line: What? Why?

dialogue.speaker: April Ludgate
dialogue.line: You'll look like a nerd.

dialogue.speaker: Andy Dwyer
dialogue.line: I am a nerd.

dialogue.speaker: April Ludgate
dialogue.line: Exactly. And I married you despite that, not because of it.

jokes.text: Doctor's response: 'Well, I can help you with the thumb. And I'll have to give you referrals for specialists for the other thousand things.' / Andy: 'Wow, thanks for nothing, Dr. Harris.' / Dr. Harris: 'You're welcome.'
jokes.setup: Andy demanded to be fixed after listing a thousand problems
jokes.punchline: The doctor's 'other thousand things' hyperbole, Andy's sarcastic 'thanks for nothing,' and the doctor's straight-faced 'you're welcome' create a triple payoff
jokes.explanation: The doctor's deadpan 'You're welcome' in response to 'thanks for nothing' is the sharpest moment of the three-part payoff. It's a perfect use of the straight-man character — he's not rattled, he's just done.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I don't like glasses.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Yeah, I don't like them either. I'm worried the doctor's gonna be really upset.

jokes.text: Bobby Newport's third campaign ad: 'Hi, I'm Bobby Newport. I'm a regular guy. I like dogs. I'm here with my Persian greyhound Raclette, who was given to me by my buddy, the pretender to the crown of Alsace-Lorraine.'
jokes.setup: A campaign ad opens with Bobby claiming to be 'a regular guy'
jokes.punchline: His 'regular guy' credentials include a Persian greyhound named Raclette (a French cheese), gifted by a European royal claimant
jokes.explanation: This is the best Bobby Newport joke in the episode. The structure is perfect: establish a relatable premise ('regular guy,' 'I like dogs'), then immediately destroy it with layers of absurd wealth and privilege — a Persian greyhound, a French cheese name, a royal pretender. Each detail is more specific and funnier than the last. 'The pretender to the crown of Alsace-Lorraine' is a particularly inspired detail — it's not even a real king, it's a claimant to a disputed historical region. Brilliant writing.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: Bobby Newport's got great herr. I mean hair. No wait, herr. That's how they say it in Europe, so it's cooler.

jokes.text: Tom's confession about not wanting to take sides: 'Leslie, I love your idea. I also love your idea. Two great ideas, two great people. I don't know which idea's better, but I do know I'll end up on the winning side. When I bet on horses, I never lose. Why? I bet on all the horses.'
jokes.setup: Tom is asked to weigh in as communications director on whether to do a positive or negative ad
jokes.punchline: His elaborate non-answer culminates in the horse-betting metaphor — he bets on all horses to ensure he never loses
jokes.explanation: The horse-betting metaphor is an excellent comedic construction — Tom's self-serving logic is internally consistent and absurd at the same time. Betting on all horses to 'never lose' is a perfect encapsulation of his character: he reframes his cowardice as strategy. Highly quotable and character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry Gergich
dialogue.line: Congressman Newport. Congressman Newport. Congress... man... Newport.

jokes.text: The public works budget meeting: Ron's immediate pivot — 'The important thing is the dam is never happening and your dream has been crushed. We're very sorry.' / 'I am not.'
jokes.setup: Chris is trying to soften the blow of cancelling all public works projects
jokes.punchline: Ron undercuts Chris's diplomatic 'we're very sorry' with an immediate 'I am not' — plus his brutal framing: 'your dream has been crushed'
jokes.explanation: The Chris/Ron dynamic is at its best here. Chris's diplomatic politeness ('We're very sorry') immediately countered by Ron's honest 'I am not' is a perfect two-beat joke. But what elevates it is Ron's preceding line: 'your dream has been crushed' — he doesn't soften the blow at all, adding extra cruelty with complete satisfaction. Excellent economy and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry Gergich
dialogue.line: I can't believe this is happening. Everything's falling apart. My career is over, my reputation is ruined, and I don't know how I'm going to face anyone ever again.

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: It's gonna be fine, Jerry.

jokes.text: Tom's talking head: 'Leslie, I love your idea. I also love your idea.' — then admitting he'll always end up on the winning side
jokes.setup: Tom is asked to weigh in as communications director on Leslie vs. Ben's competing ad strategies
jokes.punchline: He endorses both ideas with equal enthusiasm, revealing he has no actual opinion — just self-interest
jokes.explanation: The setup for the horse-betting punchline in joke #35. Works as a standalone beat but is more of a buildup than a complete joke on its own. Character consistent.

dialogue.speaker: Chris Traeger
dialogue.line: What are you going to order, Ron? Something raw and cucumber-based?

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: I'll have a cucumber.

jokes.text: Leslie assigning teams: 'Sure, I'll pick Ann and Donna for my team. You can take Jerry.' / Ben's shocked 'What?' / Leslie: 'Well, you wanted to go negative. You got the biggest negative in the world, buddy.'
jokes.setup: The group splits into teams to make demo ads; Leslie chooses her team first
jokes.punchline: Jerry is assigned to the 'negative' team as the living embodiment of negativity
jokes.explanation: The Jerry punchline is well-constructed — Leslie uses 'negative' both as an ad style and as a personal characteristic. 'The biggest negative in the world, buddy' is a perfectly delivered insult that the show earns through seasons of Jerry-mockery. The 'buddy' is a nice casual cruelty touch.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: I don't remember agreeing to this lunch. Did you drug me?

dialogue.speaker: Chris Traeger
dialogue.line: What? No, Ron, I didn't drug you.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: Then how did I get here? I have no recollection of the last two hours.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: And my drink tastes like it has a memory-altering substance in it.

jokes.text: Leslie's pep talk to her filming team: 'Think of this as Christmas and your birthday and the first day of school all rolled up into one.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is rallying her team to film a positive campaign ad
jokes.punchline: Her list of 'exciting things' to imagine includes 'the first day of school' — which most people find stressful, not joyful — delivered with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: The 'first day of school' detail is a nice Leslie touch — she genuinely loved school and doesn't clock that it's not universally joyful. Mild laugh, character-appropriate.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: I'm Leslie Knope, and I support the following things: a strong public sector, women's rights, environmental protection, education, affordable housing, and hot dogs.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Wait, why did I say hot dogs?

dialogue.speaker: Off-screen voice
dialogue.line: You like hot dogs!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: That's not a political position!

jokes.text: Leslie's Barack Obama vs. Ben Wyatt comparison: 'Barack Obama said, "Yes we can," and now he's president. Ben says, "No we shouldn't," and now he's working for his girlfriend.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is making the case for positivity in campaigning
jokes.punchline: Ben's campaign slogan would be 'No we shouldn't,' and his career status is reduced to 'working for his girlfriend'
jokes.explanation: The structural parallel is excellent — Obama/yes-we-can vs. Ben/no-we-shouldn't is a beautifully constructed political jab. The kicker ('working for his girlfriend') is the real punchline and it's a sharp, character-specific burn that also reveals Leslie's self-awareness about their situation. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: Look, I'm not going to lie to you. That was... that was really bad.

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: Like, impressively bad. I didn't know it was possible to be that bad.

jokes.text: Bobby Newport's bus appearing in the shot of Leslie's positive ad filming
jokes.setup: Leslie is filming a positive, optimistic campaign ad outdoors
jokes.punchline: Her opponent's bus drives through the shot, literally invading her space even in her best moment
jokes.explanation: A clean visual gag — the rich opponent's campaign infrastructure literally crashing into Leslie's grassroots effort is good visual metaphor comedy. Earns a rewatch bonus for the visual.

dialogue.speaker: Andy Dwyer
dialogue.line: They microwaved my arm.

dialogue.speaker: April Ludgate
dialogue.line: You mean X-rayed.

dialogue.speaker: Andy Dwyer
dialogue.line: That's what I said. They also ran some tests for science.

dialogue.speaker: April Ludgate
dialogue.line: For medical reasons.

dialogue.speaker: Andy Dwyer
dialogue.line: Yeah, that too.

jokes.text: The eye chart scene: 'E, H, 4, M. Potato shape. Coffee mug shape. Smudge, smudge, middle finger, smudge. The rest are all smudges.'
jokes.setup: Andy is reading an eye chart at an optometrist
jokes.punchline: His reading devolves from letters to shapes to the impossibility of 'middle finger' as an eye chart entry, then gives up entirely with 'the rest are all smudges'
jokes.explanation: The eye chart routine escalates beautifully: real letters, then wrong answers, then a shape description, then 'middle finger' (implying Andy sees a rude gesture or is describing an ambiguous symbol), then total surrender. The progression is perfectly timed comedy escalation. 'Middle finger' as an optometrist chart entry is the peak absurdist moment.

dialogue.speaker: Andy Dwyer
dialogue.line: Wait, you weren't actually a doctor?

dialogue.speaker: Unknown Character
dialogue.line: No, I'm not a doctor.

dialogue.speaker: Andy Dwyer
dialogue.line: But you've been describing all these medical procedures like you knew what you were talking about!

dialogue.speaker: Unknown Character
dialogue.line: I watched a lot of Grey's Anatomy.

dialogue.speaker: Andy Dwyer
dialogue.line: Oh my God.

jokes.text: April: 'Oh, my God, you drove us here. We made, like, 100 million doctors' appointments for ourselves in one week. After this we won't have to go to the doctor for, like, ten years, because we're smart.'
jokes.setup: The couple has been visiting multiple specialists
jokes.punchline: April frames their insurance-exploitation binge as strategic long-term planning, calling it 'smart'
jokes.explanation: April and Andy's twisted logic — exploiting insurance they don't understand as a form of cleverness — is good character comedy. '100 million' as a number is a fun April exaggeration.

dialogue.speaker: Announcer
dialogue.line: This ad was paid for by the Committee to Elect Leslie Knope.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: I'm Leslie Knope and I approve this message.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Wait, no I don't!

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: Leslie, what are you doing?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: I'm not letting this ad air. This is a negative ad and I don't do negative ads.

jokes.text: Andy's response to April's divorce threat: 'Well, you heard her, doc. Too handsome for glasses, no offense.'
jokes.setup: April threatens divorce if Andy gets glasses
jokes.punchline: Andy immediately cites April's authority and translates her threat into a medical directive, adding 'no offense' to the doctor
jokes.explanation: Andy's complete deference to April's medical authority ('too handsome for glasses') and the polite 'no offense' to the actual doctor is a great character beat. He's genuinely trying to be nice to the doctor while dismissing his professional opinion in favor of his wife's vanity ruling.

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: I have some good news and some bad news.

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: The good news is, the bad news isn't as bad as it could be.

jokes.text: April threatening divorce if Andy gets glasses: 'If you get glasses, I'll divorce you.' / Andy immediately: 'Well, you heard her, doc. Too handsome for glasses, no offense.'
jokes.setup: The doctor tells Andy he needs glasses
jokes.punchline: April's ultimatum is taken as medical instruction by Andy, who relays it to the doctor as if it's a clinical constraint, then adds 'no offense' to the doctor
jokes.explanation: April's controlling absurdism (divorce over glasses) perfectly matches Andy's complete acceptance of it. 'Well, you heard her, doc' is a great delivery beat — Andy treats April's whims as binding medical advice. 'No offense' is a nice small button.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: I'm so sorry I tackled you.

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: It's okay. I mean, I'm not a physical person. I'm more of a... spreadsheet guy.

jokes.text: Ben's voice-over coaching for the negative ad: multiple takes escalating from weak to increasingly over-the-top, ending with everyone just yelling 'BOBBY. NEWPORT. BOBBY. NEWPORT.'
jokes.setup: Ben is coaching Jerry to do a dramatic voice-over for the attack ad
jokes.punchline: Each take gets more theatrical until they've abandoned any semblance of an actual sentence and are just yelling the name in fragments
jokes.explanation: The escalation of the voice-over attempts, ending in the full disintegration of the sentence into isolated name-fragments, is a solid escalation bit. Gets funnier with each iteration as it becomes more absurd. Ben's direction ('give it more attitude, it's gotta scare people') frames the absurdity well.

dialogue.speaker: April Ludgate
dialogue.line: I would help you, but I'm going to get ice cream first. My priorities are pretty clear.

jokes.text: Chris inviting Ron to lunch: 'I don't know what happened. I declined his invitation. He started laughing. And the next thing I knew, we were at lunch. Did he drug me?'
jokes.setup: Ron describes how he ended up at lunch with Chris despite not wanting to go
jokes.punchline: Ron's confusion about how Chris's positivity overcame his resistance culminates in 'Did he drug me?' — a genuine inquiry
jokes.explanation: Ron's inability to process how social pressure works is a great character beat. That he would literally consider drugging as the explanation for being outmaneuvered is perfect Ron logic. The talking-head delivery makes it land as a genuine confession of bewilderment.

dialogue.speaker: Andy Dwyer
dialogue.line: Wait, we have insurance? So why do we owe $500?

dialogue.speaker: Andy Dwyer
dialogue.line: That's what insurance is for. It's like... it's like a shield made of money that protects you from having to spend money.

jokes.text: Chris at lunch: 'What are you gonna have?' / Ron: 'I'm thinking something raw and cucumber-based.' [pause] / Chris/audience: A cucumber.
jokes.setup: Chris cheerfully asks Ron what he's ordering at a restaurant
jokes.punchline: Ron's elaborate food description ('something raw and cucumber-based') is revealed to simply mean 'a cucumber' — he wants to order a whole cucumber at a restaurant
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes. The construction is perfect: 'something raw and cucumber-based' sounds like it could be a refined dish (gazpacho? tartare?) before being deflated to just an unadorned cucumber. Ron ordering a cucumber at a restaurant is both character-perfect (minimalism, distrust of culinary pretension) and a great anti-joke. High economy — the pause before the reveal does tremendous work.

dialogue.speaker: Andy Dwyer
dialogue.line: I'm not paying this medical bill. I'm just gonna run out of here!

dialogue.speaker: Andy Dwyer
dialogue.line: They can't catch me, I'm fast.

dialogue.speaker: Andy Dwyer
dialogue.line: Ow! Ow! My leg! I think I pulled something!

dialogue.speaker: Andy Dwyer
dialogue.line: I need a doctor!

jokes.text: Leslie's terrible ad: listing 'propositions 45, 86, and 102f' and 'things I am pro' with a list that includes hot dogs, while never mentioning she's running for city council
jokes.setup: Leslie presents her positive campaign ad to the group
jokes.punchline: The ad is a self-parody of Leslie's over-enthusiasm — she lists obscure local propositions, then pivots to liking hot dogs, and never once mentions she's running for office
jokes.explanation: The ad perfectly encapsulates Leslie's flaw: she is so deep in policy details and enthusiasm that she loses the forest for the trees. Propositions 45, 86, and 102f are a great detail (specific enough to be absurd), and the pivot to hot dogs ('Here are some other things I'm pro') is a wonderful escalation of absurdity. The reveal that she never mentioned city council is the structural punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Bobby Newport
dialogue.line: Well, I think the most important thing is... uh... I haven't really thought about it. I mean, I've got some ideas, but they're mostly just things my dad told me to say. Actually, no, I don't even remember those.

jokes.text: Post-screening: 'You literally never said the words city council. I did... it's implied.'
jokes.setup: Ben points out that Leslie's ad never mentioned she was running for office
jokes.punchline: Leslie's defensive 'it's implied' after being caught out — she genuinely believes this is a reasonable position
jokes.explanation: Leslie's 'it's implied' defense is pitch-perfect — she's never wrong in her own mind, even when objectively wrong. The small 'I did... it's implied' hesitation suggests she knows she's wrong but can't admit it. Great Leslie character work in minimal words.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: Chris, I'd like you to meet Jerry Gergich, our Parks Department... wait, no. Gary. Gary Gergich.

dialogue.speaker: Chris Traeger
dialogue.line: I thought his name was Jerry?

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: It is. I just like to call him Gary to hurt his feelings.

jokes.text: Tom's talking head after watching both ads: 'Leslie is so good at so many things and so bad at that.'
jokes.setup: Both ads have been screened; Leslie's was clearly a disaster
jokes.punchline: Tom's confessional is a beautifully balanced backhanded observation — he leads with praise before the knife
jokes.explanation: Excellent economy — the sentence structure (good at so many things / so bad at that) is the perfect backhanded compliment. Tom's ability to say brutal things in the most Tom-like diplomatic non-diplomatic way is character-consistent.

dialogue.speaker: Kyle
dialogue.line: I'm not really interested in Japanese culture. I just needed a job.

jokes.text: Ben's attack ad: 'Bobby Newport's never had a real job in his life. His cushy job at his dad's candy company, handed to him. His 60-foot boat, Bobby's boat, handed to him when he was 12.'
jokes.setup: Ben's attack ad is screened for the group
jokes.punchline: The straight-faced attack ad works as comedy because the things being called out (boat at age 12, candy company job) are so absurdly privileged they critique themselves
jokes.explanation: The ad is funny because the facts about Bobby's privilege are so egregious they're self-satirizing. A 60-foot boat named 'Bobby's boat' at age 12 is a perfectly chosen detail. Functional political satire.

dialogue.speaker: Bobby Newport
dialogue.line: Leslie, please just quit the race.

dialogue.speaker: Bobby Newport
dialogue.line: Just quit. Just quit, quit, quit, quit.

dialogue.speaker: Bobby Newport
dialogue.line: Quit quit quit quit quit quit quit.

dialogue.speaker: Bobby Newport
dialogue.line: Why won't you quit?

dialogue.speaker: Bobby Newport
dialogue.line: Quit!

jokes.text: Ann's confessional about Leslie: 'Leslie is so good at so many things and so bad at that.'
jokes.setup: We've just watched Leslie's chaotically unfocused positive campaign ad
jokes.punchline: Ann's perfectly calibrated talking head that acknowledges Leslie's gifts while landing the joke with maximum economy
jokes.explanation: Economy is exceptional — this is a 14-word sentence that perfectly captures the whole comedic situation. 'So good at so many things and so bad at that' balances affection and roasting perfectly. Ann as Leslie's best friend/truth-teller makes this the ideal voice for the observation.

dialogue.speaker: Bobby Newport
dialogue.line: Well, my dad said I should run for something, and politics seemed easier than a actual business.

jokes.text: Ben's ad closing: 'Bobby Newport wants you to just hand him this election. Don't.' — voice-over: 'I won't.'
jokes.setup: The attack ad builds to its conclusion about Newport being handed things
jokes.punchline: The sudden first-person 'I won't' from the narrator — unexpectedly personal and slightly unhinged in the context of a campaign ad
jokes.explanation: The sudden shift from 'don't' (addressing the voter) to 'I won't' (the narrator becoming personally invested) is a subtle but funny structural joke. It suggests Ben may have put a bit too much of himself into the ad. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Bobby Newport
dialogue.line: Look, Leslie, I'm a reasonable guy. Let's compromise. You keep doing your job, and I'll take all the credit and the salary.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: That's not a compromise, Bobby. That's just you being you.

jokes.text: Leslie's horrified response to Ben's ad: 'It's depressing. It's awful. I am Ben Wyatt, and I want to destroy Leslie's dreams.'
jokes.setup: Everyone else loves Ben's attack ad; Leslie hates it
jokes.punchline: Leslie projects her feelings onto Ben in the most melodramatic way: he wants to 'destroy her dreams'
jokes.explanation: Leslie ventriloquizing Ben's sinister inner monologue is a good character beat. The specific phrasing 'destroy Leslie's dreams' is the right level of melodrama for her character. The joke lands because we know Leslie genuinely feels this way.

dialogue.speaker: Bobby Newport
dialogue.line: Wait, how were you yourself as a child?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: What do you mean?

dialogue.speaker: Bobby Newport
dialogue.line: Well, you're not yourself now.

jokes.text: Andy's medical summary: 'I got my ankles microwaved. They took my blood away to use for science. April had her sinuses removed.'
jokes.setup: Andy and April recap their week of medical appointments
jokes.punchline: Andy's description of routine medical procedures is hilariously wrong: ankles were X-rayed (not microwaved), blood was taken for cholesterol tests (not science), sinuses were examined (not removed)
jokes.explanation: Andy's malapropisms for medical procedures are inventively wrong in exactly the right way. 'Microwaved' for X-rayed, 'used for science' for cholesterol test, and 'sinuses removed' for examined are three distinct jokes in quick succession. Each one escalates the wrongness.

dialogue.speaker: Andy Dwyer
dialogue.line: We could treat each other's injuries ourselves. It'd be like being our own doctors.

dialogue.speaker: April Ludgate
dialogue.line: That does sound romantic. Like we're living under a bridge, performing surgery with a bottle cap and whatever we find in the dirt.

jokes.text: Andy: 'Some guy looked at my wiener, touched it. That was weird. And that guy wasn't even a doctor. That... what?'
jokes.setup: Andy is cataloguing his medical appointment experiences
jokes.punchline: He casually mentions a stranger touched him inappropriately, then the beat where he processes that the person wasn't a doctor
jokes.explanation: The structure is excellent: Andy mentions it casually as part of a list, then he — and the audience — realizes what he's just said. 'That... what?' is the perfect confused self-interrogation. The joke is character-specific because only Andy would process this so slowly and tell it so casually. Good cringe-comedy construction.

jokes.text: Leslie physically tackling Ben to prevent him delivering the DVD to the station, then lying on the ground: 'I am Leslie Knope, and I do not approve this message.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has reluctantly agreed to air Ben's attack ad but as the deadline arrives, she panics
jokes.punchline: She tackles Ben on the way to the control room, then while lying on the ground delivers a parody of the standard 'I approve this message' disclaimer
jokes.explanation: The physical comedy of Leslie tackling Ben is funny on its own, but the real joke is the parody of the campaign ad disclaimer delivered from the floor. 'I do not approve this message' as a line is brilliantly constructed — it inverts the formulaic political phrase in a way that's both funny and character-revealing. High quotability, excellent structure, perfect character integration. One of the episode's best moments.

jokes.text: Tom's reaction to the news that neither ad aired and they can't get money back: 'You both really blew this. But I can't wait to hear your new ideas. I love 'em already. Ooh, I'm hungry. Tommy needs a mango. See ya.'
jokes.setup: The bad news is delivered that both ads failed and the money is gone
jokes.punchline: Tom pivots from faux-supportive ('I can't wait to hear your new ideas, I love 'em already') to completely checked-out ('Tommy needs a mango') in about three seconds
jokes.explanation: 'Tommy needs a mango' is a beautifully specific exit line. Tom referring to himself in third person while abandoning the team is perfect Tom Haverford. The rapid transition from faux-helpful to self-interested is very well-timed.

jokes.text: Tom's spin after both ads fail to air: 'But you know what, I can't wait to hear your new ideas. I love 'em already. Ooh, I'm hungry. Tommy needs a mango. See ya.'
jokes.setup: Tom has just delivered bad news that neither ad aired and they can't get the money back
jokes.punchline: Tom pivots from news delivery to false enthusiasm for future ideas to immediate abandonment ('Tommy needs a mango. See ya.')
jokes.explanation: 'Tommy needs a mango. See ya.' is a great character exit. Tom's self-absorption is performed in third person (referring to himself as 'Tommy'), and his pivot from campaign crisis to personal snack needs is perfectly Tom. The 'I love 'em already' without hearing any ideas is also good character comedy.

jokes.text: Ben: 'I bet in your dreams you weren't losing an election by 70 points.' / Leslie: 'You were pretty easy to take down.' / Ben: 'Thanks.'
jokes.setup: Ben is gently challenging Leslie to be tougher; Leslie just tackled him to the floor
jokes.punchline: Ben's 'Thanks' in response to being called 'easy to take down' — he accepts it with complete resigned deadpan
jokes.explanation: Ben's one-word 'Thanks' after being reminded he just got physically taken down by his girlfriend is a good deadpan button. Small joke but well-timed.

jokes.text: Chris inviting Ron to a Japanese tea ceremony seminar; Ron declining citing 'we did just have lunch last week, so I feel like we've spent enough social time together for the foreseeable... ever.'
jokes.setup: Chris enthusiastically invites Ron to a cultural enrichment event, noting he values silence
jokes.punchline: Ron's declining pivot ends with '...for the foreseeable... ever' — a perfectly constructed trailing-off that makes 'ever' the punchline
jokes.explanation: The construction of '...for the foreseeable... ever' is the joke — Ron begins a polite decline ('foreseeable future') and then decides even that's too open-ended and closes it permanently. The ellipsis-then-'ever' structure is excellent. Pure Ron Swanson economy of antisocial expression.

jokes.text: Donna: 'Maybe he just misses his little buddy.' / Ron reacts with visible physical discomfort. 'Ow.'
jokes.setup: Donna suggests Chris might miss Ben and see Ron as a replacement friend
jokes.punchline: Ron's entire response is 'Ow' — a physical reaction to the suggestion of being someone's buddy, as if the very concept caused pain
jokes.explanation: One syllable. Maximum character comedy. 'Ow' as Ron's reaction to being called a 'little buddy' is physically perfect — Nick Offerman's delivery of pained resignation makes the joke. Character integration is near-perfect: this is Ron Swanson distilled to a single phoneme. Economy score is 10. This is comparable in quality to 'Present' — both are one-word jokes that do tremendous character work.

jokes.text: Andy and April's medical bill standoff: 'Whoa, yeah, won't be needing that. I've got the free medicine card.' / 'There's a $500 deductible.' / 'I think you're wrong. We have the insurance thing. I believe we're covered.'
jokes.setup: Andy and April arrived at the doctor thinking they had full insurance coverage
jokes.punchline: Andy refers to insurance as 'the free medicine card' and confidently disputes the doctor's correct explanation of a deductible
jokes.explanation: 'The free medicine card' is a great Andy coinage — it perfectly captures how someone with zero financial literacy would conceptualize health insurance. The escalating confidence despite being wrong ('I think you're wrong,' 'I believe we're covered') is consistent character comedy.

jokes.text: Andy and April dine-and-dash from the doctor's office: 'Let's go! Dine and dash! Out of the way! Yeah! Whoo-hoo-hoo!'
jokes.setup: Andy and April can't pay the $500 deductible
jokes.punchline: Their solution is to literally run out of the medical office shouting 'dine and dash' — a restaurant term applied to a medical context
jokes.explanation: The 'dine and dash' terminology applied to a medical office is a perfect Andy brain construction. Their complete commitment to the exit (shouting 'whoo-hoo-hoo') makes it infectious. Good physical comedy energy.

jokes.text: Andy immediately runs into an ambulance outside and shouts: 'Call an ambulance! A different ambulance than the one I ran into.'
jokes.setup: Andy and April flee the medical office in triumph
jokes.punchline: Andy immediately injures himself on an ambulance, then — while calling for medical help — specifies he wants a DIFFERENT ambulance from the one he damaged
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best joke. The structure is impeccable: the irony of fleeing a doctor's office and immediately needing an ambulance is perfect, but the specification 'a different ambulance than the one I ran into' elevates it from a good situational joke to a classic. That qualifier — worrying about the ambulance he damaged rather than his own injury — reveals Andy's scrambled priorities perfectly. It's also the logical culmination of the entire Andy/April medical subplot. High quotability, deserves 9+ comparison.

jokes.text: Leslie's childhood ad: ten-year-old Leslie proposing 'a more progressive tax on residential properties'
jokes.setup: Ben uses archive footage of Leslie as a ten-year-old for the homemade attack ad
jokes.punchline: Child Leslie's campaign platform includes a 'progressive tax on residential properties' — a highly specific policy position for a ten-year-old
jokes.explanation: The joke works on multiple levels: it's funny that a child made a political ad at all, funnier that it includes 'progressive residential tax,' and funniest because it makes perfect sense for who Leslie Knope is. It confirms that Leslie has always been Leslie. Character integration is exceptional — this joke could only work with this character.

jokes.text: Bobby Newport in the ad: 'People keep asking me: Bobby, what are you gonna do once you get into office? Um, I'm pretty sure I'll figure it out.'
jokes.setup: The homemade attack ad contrasts Leslie-at-ten with Bobby-today
jokes.punchline: Bobby's entire policy platform is 'I'm pretty sure I'll figure it out' — supreme confidence in improvisation with zero preparation
jokes.explanation: This is the perfect contrast joke — child Leslie's progressive tax policy vs. adult Bobby's 'I'll figure it out.' The line is also a sharp satirical take on certain real-world political candidates. 'I'm pretty sure I'll figure it out' is extremely quotable and a great encapsulation of Bobby's entire character.

jokes.text: The ad's closing: 'They do have one thing in common.' / Young Leslie and Bobby both say: 'I like dogs.' / 'Vote Knope for city council.'
jokes.setup: The ad has been contrasting Leslie and Bobby as polar opposites
jokes.punchline: The one thing they share is the most benign possible common ground: both like dogs
jokes.explanation: The callback to Bobby's 'I like dogs' from his earlier campaign ad is satisfying. The joke works as anti-climax — after establishing the enormous gulf between the candidates, the one bridge is something completely trivial. The split-screen/parallel delivery amplifies the irony.

jokes.text: Ron introducing Kyle to Chris: 'This is a great friend of mine. He is a fellow who works in the building and he is named Dennis. Kyle.' / Kyle: 'I was eating rice, and Ron made me come up here. But sure, that sounds fun.'
jokes.setup: Ron is trying to set Chris up with someone to go to the tea ceremony instead of him
jokes.punchline: Ron's description of his 'great friend' reveals he doesn't know Kyle's name (calls him Dennis first), and Kyle's explanation makes clear Ron literally drafted him from a meal
jokes.explanation: Ron calling Kyle 'Dennis' before correcting himself reveals that he truly doesn't know who this person is — he just grabbed the nearest warm body. Kyle's deadpan 'I was eating rice, and Ron made me come up here' is a great straight-man reveal. The whole sequence exposes Ron's social maneuvering as hilariously crude.

jokes.text: Chris immediately responding 'Arigato!' to Kyle, who Ron described as a 'japanophile' because he was eating rice
jokes.setup: Ron told Chris that Kyle 'strongly enjoys Japanese culture'
jokes.punchline: Chris enthusiastically greets Kyle in Japanese based on Ron's paper-thin 'evidence' (he was eating rice)
jokes.explanation: Chris's enthusiastic acceptance of Ron's absurd framing (eating rice = japanophile) is good character comedy for both characters. Chris's optimism makes him credulous; Ron's manipulation is efficient.

jokes.text: Ron denying loneliness: 'No, no, no, no. I'm not lonely. I have me. And 4,000 Facebook friends and a hot girlfriend.'
jokes.setup: Chris suggests Ron might miss Ben and just wants a friend
jokes.punchline: Ron's flustered denial lists 'me' as his primary social network, then Facebook friends (deeply at odds with his technophobia) and his girlfriend
jokes.explanation: 'I have me' is characteristically Ron — he is his own best and sufficient companion. '4,000 Facebook friends' is funny because Ron is so anti-technology, anti-social media that having 4,000 Facebook friends seems completely implausible. The defensiveness of the list reveals the insecurity beneath.

jokes.text: Ron's reveal: 'I wanted to spend time with you, because I have to replace Ben as assistant city manager and I was giving you a tryout of sorts. Now, I'll mull my options for the next few months, but I'd love you to keep an open mind.'
jokes.setup: Chris thinks Ron has been warming to friendship; Ron has been denying being lonely
jokes.punchline: Ron's real motive is revealed: he's been conducting a stealth job interview. All the lunches and invitations were professional evaluation, not friendship
jokes.explanation: The recontextualization of all Ron's interactions with Chris as a professional evaluation is a satisfying plot-comedy reveal. It's both hilarious (Ron conducted a secret hiring process through apparently accidental socializing) and completely in-character (Ron would never just admit he wants to hang out). Good callback payoff.

jokes.text: Bobby Newport confronting Leslie and Ben about the video: 'Why'd you guys post that video of me, man? I mean, that didn't make me feel good. It was mean. You guys are mean.'
jokes.setup: Bobby shows up at the restaurant where Leslie and Ben are working
jokes.punchline: His political grievance is expressed with the emotional vocabulary of a middle schooler: 'You guys are mean'
jokes.explanation: Bobby's political confrontation using playground language is consistently funny. 'You guys are mean' from a man running for elected office lands because of the sincerity — he genuinely feels this way and has no better framework for expressing it.

jokes.text: Bobby Newport asking Leslie and Ben to quit the campaign: 'Just stop running, okay? Just... that... stop. Stop running the ad? No, stop running the campaign. What? Just quit. It would be so cool of you if you just quit. Then I can win the election, and I'll have a big party, and I'll put you both on the guest list, plus one. I'm gonna have a man who does magic.'
jokes.setup: Bobby has a legitimate political complaint about the attack video
jokes.punchline: His solution is to simply ask them to quit, sweetening the deal with a party, plus-ones, and a magician — the incentives of an eight-year-old's birthday party
jokes.explanation: This is Bobby Newport at his absolute best. The escalation from 'just quit' to party invitation to plus-one to 'a man who does magic' (with the important qualification 'not cheesy magic, like, good magic') is sublime character comedy. Each detail reveals more about how Bobby's mind works. The magician detail is the peak — it's both absurdly generous in Bobby's framework and absurdly insufficient as political negotiation. Character integration is near-perfect; this speech could ONLY be Bobby Newport.

jokes.text: Bobby's pitch for Leslie to drop out: 'I'll put you both on the guest list, plus one. I'm gonna have a man who does magic. He's really good. Not like cheesy magic. Like, good magic.'
jokes.setup: Bobby asks Leslie to just quit the campaign so he can win and have a big party
jokes.punchline: His incentives include guest list access and a reassurance about the quality of the magic at his victory party — 'Not like cheesy magic. Like, good magic.'
jokes.explanation: This is one of the best Bobby Newport jokes in the episode. The distinction between 'cheesy magic' and 'good magic' as a negotiating point in a city council election is inspired absurdism. Bobby has no political arguments — only party logistics. And the 'good magic' qualifier shows he has standards, just wildly inappropriate ones. The whole speech ('give me it. Give me it.') combined with the magic detail makes this a standout moment.

jokes.text: Bobby's negotiation escalation: 'Give me it. Give me it. Come on, give me it. Just give me the election. I'm sorry, please. Please.' / Ben: 'Well, Leslie, he does make a compelling argument.'
jokes.setup: Bobby has finished his pitch for Leslie to quit; she's refusing
jokes.punchline: Bobby's plea devolves into pure 'give me it' repetition like a toddler, then Ben drily comments that he 'makes a compelling argument'
jokes.explanation: Bobby's devolution to 'give me it' is funny on its own, but Ben's perfectly straight 'he does make a compelling argument' is the real punchline. The ironic endorsement of Bobby's toddler-level logic is a great Ben Wyatt deadpan moment.

jokes.text: Bobby banging his hand on the table: 'Ah, it's not padded!'
jokes.setup: Bobby is frustrated that Leslie won't quit; he slams his hand on the table for emphasis
jokes.punchline: The table is not padded (as presumably his tables at home are), and he's genuinely surprised and hurt
jokes.explanation: 'It's not padded!' is a brilliant small joke. It implies Bobby's home life includes padded surfaces everywhere — a world so cushioned by wealth that the contact of a normal table is shocking. The complaint reveals more about his life than many full scenes could. Exceptional character integration and economy.

jokes.text: Ben's deadpan: 'Well, Leslie, he does make a compelling argument.'
jokes.setup: Bobby has just whined 'give me it' repeatedly and begged Leslie to quit
jokes.punchline: Ben treating this toddler tantrum as a 'compelling argument'
jokes.explanation: Perfect deadpan button on Bobby's begging sequence. Four words doing maximum work. Ben's straight-man neutrality turns the entire moment into irony without drawing attention away from Bobby.

jokes.text: Bobby: 'I need something to do to get my dad off my back. This seemed easy. What about you, why are you doing it? Who's your dad?'
jokes.setup: Leslie asks Bobby why he's running for office; he answers honestly
jokes.punchline: Bobby immediately assumes Leslie's motivation is also parental pressure, asking 'Who's your dad?' — unable to conceive that someone would run for civic reasons
jokes.explanation: 'Who's your dad?' is an inspired line — Bobby's worldview is so thoroughly dynastic that civic motivation is literally incomprehensible to him. It also inadvertently reveals his own psychology (everything is about his dad). Economy and character integration are both excellent.

jokes.text: Bobby's counter-proposal: 'How 'bout you quit running, then I win, but then I let you do all the work.'
jokes.setup: Leslie explains she's running to improve people's lives; Bobby considers this
jokes.punchline: Bobby solves the conflict with a proposal: she quits, he wins the title, but she can do the actual governing — he wants the win without the work
jokes.explanation: Bobby's 'solution' is accidentaly insightful about how some politicians operate while being funny as a character beat. He wants the title and the party; she can have the governance. It's absurd yet has satirical bite.

jokes.text: Bobby's reaction after Leslie and Ben leave: 'Why are you guys smiling? I feel bad.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has stood up to Bobby and they leave confident; Bobby's team apparently smiles
jokes.punchline: Bobby's complete inability to understand why anyone would be pleased — he's still processing that he didn't get what he wanted
jokes.explanation: A good character button — Bobby's emotional simplicity ('I feel bad') as his team presumably smiles at his opponent's fire is endearing and funny. Slight joke but consistent character work.

jokes.text: Bobby asking about the little girl in Leslie's video: 'Oh, my God, she's so cute. Do you think you can talk to her and let her do an ad for me?' / Leslie: 'That girl is me as a ten-year-old.' / Bobby: 'How'd you do that?'
jokes.setup: Bobby watched the attack ad featuring young Leslie
jokes.punchline: Bobby wants to recruit young Leslie for his own ad, not understanding that the footage is historical; when told she IS that girl, he asks 'How'd you do that?' as if it's a magic trick
jokes.explanation: 'How'd you do that?' is a perfect punchline — Bobby cannot process the concept of archive footage or the passage of time, and his bewilderment is completely genuine. It also serves as a commentary on Bobby's intellectual limitations while being a great callback to the ad. One of the episode's most quotable lines. The setup (wanting to hire child Leslie) is already funny before the punchline.

jokes.text: Ben's advice: 'Maybe you should see one of the other doctors.' (to Bobby after 'How'd you do that?')
jokes.setup: Bobby has just asked 'How'd you do that?' about Leslie being the same person as her ten-year-old self in a video
jokes.punchline: Ben's gentle recommendation that Bobby needs medical evaluation, delivered with complete deadpan sincerity
jokes.explanation: A good button on the 'How'd you do that' joke. Ben's straight-faced medical referral is a nice callback to the Andy/doctor subplot while also being a character beat for Ben as the pragmatic straight-man.

jokes.text: Andy: 'No more doctors. They're a bunch of scam artists. They reel you in with the free stuff. Next thing you know, bam, you run into an ambulance. Every time.'
jokes.setup: April wants to get Andy more medical care
jokes.punchline: Andy has concluded that doctors are scammers based on his experience, and 'running into an ambulance' is apparently a pattern that happens 'every time'
jokes.explanation: The callback to the ambulance incident works beautifully here. 'Every time' implies this has happened on multiple prior occasions, which retroactively makes the joke even better. Andy's logic chain ('they reel you in with free stuff → you run into an ambulance → scam artists') is perfectly nonsensical. 'Every time' is the best two words of the episode.

jokes.text: Andy: 'We could buy a sewing kit. You could sew up my lip underneath a bridge somewhere.' / April: 'Mmm, so romantic.'
jokes.setup: Andy and April discuss alternatives to going back to the doctor
jokes.punchline: April finds 'sewing up my lip under a bridge' genuinely romantic — it perfectly matches her gothic/unconventional sensibility
jokes.explanation: This is a beautiful April/Andy character moment. April's 'Mmm, so romantic' is genuine — she actually finds this scenario appealing. The contrast between the objectively grim scenario (sewing a wound under a bridge) and her sincere enthusiasm is the joke, but it's also weirdly tender. Character integration for both is excellent: this dynamic is uniquely theirs.

jokes.text: The closing exchange: Andy: 'Do you think sewing kits are covered by insurance? Or groceries or, like, Xbox games?' / April: 'What is insurance?' / Andy: 'I don't know. Who cares?'
jokes.setup: The Andy/April subplot has been about their fundamental misunderstanding of insurance
jokes.punchline: The episode closes with April asking 'What is insurance?' — having been through a full day of medical appointments — and Andy's philosophical dismissal: 'I don't know. Who cares?'
jokes.explanation: A perfect closing joke for the subplot. After an entire episode of medical chaos caused by their ignorance about insurance, April still doesn't know what it is, and Andy's response ('I don't know. Who cares?') is the most Andy possible resolution. The Xbox games and groceries listed as potentially insurable is a great detail — it shows their thinking hasn't progressed at all. Economy is excellent; the callback is satisfying.

tmdb_overview: Faced with a tough new opponent, Leslie and Ben disagree on the content of her first campaign ad. Ron is very uncomfortable when Chris tries to befriend him, while Andy and April make a trip to the doctor.
insight: Campaign ad shooting exposes Leslie's control issues through relentless cringe across fifty-five jokes.
